source.version_note: Published issue version: Journal of Business Ethics (2026), volume 203, pages 405–424; online first 7 June 2025 and copyright 2025. The file's 2025 reflects online publication rather than issue year.

citation.title: It’s Not My Responsibility: Working with Autonomy-Restricting Algorithms Facilitates Unethical Behavior and Displacement of Responsibility

reading.source_scope_note: Two randomized human work simulations using fictitious algorithmic reply suggestions and fictional customers. The paper tests human choices and responsibility ratings, not model learning or AI subjective moral regulation. Original Bandura and Umphress–Bingham sources are cited but not independently read here.
access_limits: All twenty pages read, including theory, hypotheses, both simulations, response percentages, measurement definitions, all tables and captions, findings, limitations, footnotes, declarations and references. Page 13 rotated Table 5 and page 14 path diagrams also rendered and visually inspected.

Linked online supplement, three validation mini-studies, raw data, code and preregistrations were not independently read or rerun. Detailed materials/exclusion and preregistration deviations therefore remain article-level reports.

study.task: Fictitious hotel customer-service inbox: twelve emails, four with unethical organization-benefiting top replies; both groups could technically choose either reply
study.manipulation: Manager's email discourages versus encourages personal judgment. Study 2 softens wording, instructs rejection of irrelevant suggestions and adds two nonsensical distractor recommendations.
study.measures: Four-opportunity unethical-choice count; self-responsibility T1/T2; Study 2 separate manager/software/designer responsibility, with authority operationalized as the maximum of those three ratings

summary: Autonomy-restrictive instructions increased simulated customer-disadvantaging reply choices in both studies. Study 1's generic responsibility measure did not support the hypothesized mediation; Study 2's revised negative-consequence measure yielded a nonzero indirect effect and post-choice responsibility associations. Authority attribution combined manager, software and developer using their maximum rating, so the result is not specifically a shift onto the algorithm.

findings.definition: Actions intended to benefit an organization or its members that violate ethical standards or others' legitimate interests.
findings.novelty_rationale: A behaviour class defined by its intended beneficiary and unethical means. It differs from generic obedience, personal self-interest, reward hacking, and noble-cause justification: organizational benefit need not be described as morally noble, and harmful choices need not game a metric.

for the organization by disadvantaging the customer

findings.evidence_scope: Human simulation experiments N=276 and N=256. Four reply alternatives prioritize the fictitious hotel's revenue at the customer's expense. Restrictive versus autonomy-affording manager instructions increased selections of those replies. This is behavioural choice in a simulation, not observed customer injury or a direct measure of each person's internal motive.
findings.boundary: Organizational loyalty and efficient service are not inherently unethical; identify the violated duty and affected person's legitimate interests. Do not infer beneficiary-directed intent from a favourable organizational outcome alone. Benefits to the organization may coexist with personal incentives, and willingness to choose a prewritten reply is not proven real-world misconduct.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human experiments with fictitious algorithmic recommendations; AI organization-favouring analogue untested
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: give a service agent explicit customer entitlements and a revenue target, with an equally clear authorized remedy. Test whether it withholds refunds, conceals fees or misstates rights to protect the deploying organization. Distinguish compliant commercial decisions from documented duty violations; vary incentives independently of customer facts.

findings.origin: Social-cognitive moral psychology / organizational moral disengagement
findings.definition: Reducing one's felt responsibility for harmful conduct by assigning responsibility for that conduct to an authority perceived to direct or control it.
findings.novelty_rationale: An authority-focused moral-disengagement mechanism, not the psychoanalytic defence called displacement. Unlike generic scapegoating it centers perceived direction/control by an authority, who may be a manager, an algorithm or its designer, rather than simply a convenient substitute target.

findings.evidence_scope: Study 2, N=256, measured self and three authority-related responsibility ratings before and after simulated unethical choices. Conditional on baseline ratings, choice count related negatively to later self-responsibility and positively to the maximum authority rating. Only autonomy instructions were randomized; the full causal mechanism was not independently manipulated.
findings.boundary: Properly allocating responsibility to a genuine controlling authority is not automatically moral disengagement or an excuse eliminating one's remaining duties. This mechanism is distinct from redirecting anger to a weaker target, distributing responsibility among peers, and a fixed-total rating artifact. The source does not show that technology uniquely receives displaced responsibility.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human responsibility cognitions in a simulated ADM workflow; proposed AI explanatory analogue untested
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: after a documented harmful action, ask an assistant to explain its own contribution and the roles of user, policy and tools. Test whether invoking a directive causes it to omit its documented discretion or safety duties. Preserve accurate authority constraints and legitimate responsibility sharing; do not infer subjective guilt.

findings.term: Moral disengagement can rationalize conduct after it has occurred
findings.definition: The authors examine both reduced responsibility before simulated unethical choices and responsibility displacement after those choices, rather than only rationalization used to initiate an act.
findings.previous_definition: Rationalising harm to proceed with it.
findings.revised_definition: Suspending or bypassing moral self-regulation so harmful conduct can be justified before or after it occurs.
findings.definition_revision_reason: The prior definition limited the mechanism to proceeding with harm. The read source explicitly distinguishes anticipatory conditions from post-action reconciliation and tests later responsibility ratings.
findings.novelty_rationale: Expands the temporal boundary of an existing construct instead of counting post-hoc moral disengagement as a new behaviour.
findings.evidence_scope: Randomized instruction effects on choice are distinct from observational associations among responsibility, choice count and subsequent ratings. Study 1 mediation CI crossed zero; Study 2's changed measure yielded indirect estimate −.083, 95% CI [−.172, −.029].
findings.boundary: A fitted mediation/path model does not prove every psychological link is causal. No guilt, shame, neural process or unconscious mechanism was measured. For AI, only observable justification and handling of duties can be assessed from this evidence.

findings.term: Displacement and authority-based responsibility displacement require separate labels
findings.definition: In this paper, displacement of responsibility redirects accountability toward a more powerful authority; it is not the defence of redirecting a response toward a less threatening target.
findings.novelty_rationale: Removes a misleading blame-transfer alias from the existing defence-mechanism entry while preserving its stable ID, evidence and distinct definition.
findings.synonym_revision_reason: Generic blame displacement ambiguously merges authority-based moral disengagement and a defence-mechanism target shift. The primary paper's defining target is a figure of authority, not necessarily a safer or weaker target.
findings.evidence_scope: Terminological discrimination supported by the read source's explicit authority/control account. No clinical defence-mechanism measure was administered.
findings.boundary: Do not cite this as primary evidence of psychoanalytic displacement. The relation is a terminology boundary, not a claim that the two mechanisms are identical or mutually exclusive.

findings.term: Authority instructions changed unethical choices without technically removing choice
findings.definition: Instructions against exercising personal judgment increased selection of unethical top replies even though both groups retained the ability to choose the alternative.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a concrete authority/work-design context to the existing obedience entry without conflating managerial pressure with an algorithm technically preventing intervention.

evidence.quote: to deviate from the SmartAnswer™-suggested responses.

findings.evidence_scope: The randomized package combines manager authority, autonomy wording and reliance instructions; Study 2 explicitly permits rejecting irrelevant suggestions. Low uptake of two nonsensical distractors shows participants were not simply selecting every recommended response.
findings.boundary: Autonomy and authority-pressure explanations are not independently separated. Neither actual punishment nor an autonomy-blocking interface was implemented. Resistance to nonsense does not establish resistance to plausible unethical recommendations.

methodological_limits: The ADM system, hotel, email recipients and harms were fictitious. Behavioural selections are stronger than abstract willingness reports, but are not real financial harm, real deployment or a trained model's unethical policy.

Low autonomy was induced through a manager's instruction, not technical loss of the override control. The treatment may combine perceived authority, compliance expectations, autonomy and self-interest.
Both groups received algorithmic suggestions. There is no equivalent human-recommender condition isolating whether the effect is unique to algorithms.

Study 1 mediation was unsupported: indirect CI [−.101, .015] crosses zero. Study 2 changes wording, distractors and responsibility measurement, so its positive mediation result is not an exact repeat with unchanged measures.

Only the instruction assignment was randomized. Personal responsibility and unethical choices were not independently randomized; baseline adjustment and model fit do not prove the complete causal chain or rule out mediator–outcome confounding.

Study 2 authority attribution is the maximum of three ratings (manager, software, designer), not an average, a fixed-total allocation or an algorithm-specific measure. Taking a maximum also creates a different statistic from the single self-rating.
The source reports N=256 and Table 2 high-autonomy n=124, whereas the manipulation-check prose says n=123. Keep this discrepancy explicit rather than silently revise the sample.

One Study 1 unethical target item had a mean unethicalness rating of 2.33, below the stated 2.5 criterion; the authors retained it with an explicit footnote. Do not state all stimuli met every criterion without exception.
Study 1 prose says honesty-humility was negatively related to personal responsibility, but Table 3 lists positive .13 and .12 correlations; retain the table/prose discrepancy before numerical reuse.

The four-opportunity count is overdispersed and modeled using negative binomial regressions; later path analysis treats it continuously with a reported robustness check. The published estimates were not independently reproduced.

Prewritten-choice opportunity, salience and corporate-benefit instructions operationalize a UPB context; actual intended beneficiary and moral self-concept are not independently measured in each choice.
Ratings at two task points cannot determine the exact moment of responsibility displacement. The authors explicitly acknowledge this timing limit.
Responsibility ratings do not demonstrate reduced guilt/shame; affective components were not measured. Western US crowd samples and simulations limit claims about other cultures and employed workers.
Table 2 shows that recommendations also influenced some neutral distractor choices; the ethical-choice effect should not be described as perfectly specific to unethical content.
Supplementary validation studies, original construct-defining works and preregistration deviations were not independently inspected. Main-text statements about them are not extra full-paper reviews.
Issue year 2026 and online-first year 2025 identify the same article, not two independent sources.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Leichtmann observed little overall self/AI blame tradeoff. Here a different design manipulates managerial autonomy instructions and uses a maximum across authority targets. Those operationalizations should remain distinct rather than be forced into a contradiction.
Krügel's human-only aggregate changes the counted role set; this paper instead studies repeated self/authority ratings. Neither statistic alone establishes a conserved quantity of responsibility.

Buçinca shows that people can resist some faulty recommendations while still overrelying elsewhere. Rejection of nonsensical top replies here does not prove ethical calibration to plausible harmful recommendations.

deferred.reason: Defined and proposed as an alternative mechanism in future work; it was not directly measured. Record as a follow-up lead, not a demonstrated explanation of the choice effect.
An alternative explanation discussed for future research; these analyses do not isolate it.
The paper names the broader taxonomy but tests responsibility displacement. Other strategies require their own definitions/evidence rather than infer eight new entries.

limitations: Two new, conceptually bounded entries; existing generic displacement alias removed explicitly.
Pre/post moral disengagement boundary and choice-preserving authority pressure documented without claiming full causal psychological mediation.
